simple: The molecule that stores genetic information.
how: Its sequence contains inherited instructions. Chromosomes package that DNA.
memory: DNA is the information; chromosomes are its packages.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A packaged DNA molecule with associated proteins.
how: It carries many genes. After replication, one duplicated chromosome has two sister chromatids.
memory: One package can have two joined copies.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A segment of DNA with a biological role.
how: Genes occupy positions on chromosomes and can be transmitted through gametes.
memory: A gene is a stretch of DNA.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A particular position on a chromosome or in a genome.
how: The gene is the DNA segment. Its locus tells you where that segment is located.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A version of a DNA sequence at a particular locus.
how: Homologous chromosomes can have different versions at the same position, illustrated by A and a.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A reproductive cell that contributes one chromosome set at fertilization.
how: In the human examples, sperm and egg each carry 23 chromosomes.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Corresponding chromosomes inherited from different parents.
how: They carry matching gene positions but can contain different alleles. They separate in meiosis I.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The two copies formed when one chromosome replicates.
how: They stay joined through meiosis I and separate in meiosis II. Crossing over can later make their DNA differ.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Copying DNA before cell division.
how: One round prepares chromosomes for both meiotic divisions. DNA quantity doubles while set number remains the same.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Having two complete chromosome sets.
how: A typical human diploid body cell has 46 chromosomes. Copying DNA does not itself add another set.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Having one complete chromosome set.
how: Human gametes have 23 chromosomes. Cells after meiosis I are haploid even though chromosomes remain duplicated.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The number of complete chromosome sets in a cell.
how: It describes sets, not the amount of copied DNA. Diploid is 2n, haploid is n.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A chromosome other than a sex chromosome.
how: A human gamete has 22 autosomes and one sex chromosome.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A chromosome involved in the chromosomal sex system.
how: The human gamete example contains one sex chromosome alongside 22 autosomes.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A body cell outside the reproductive germ-cell lineage.
how: The slides contrast typical diploid human body cells with haploid gametes.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The cell formed by fusion of two gametes.
how: Fertilization combines their chromosome contributions and restores diploidy in the human cycle.
memory: A zygote is the joined starting cell.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Fusion of gametes and their genetic contributions.
how: One haploid contribution combines with another. Random pairing of possibilities adds genetic combinations.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Cell division that generally preserves chromosome-set number.
how: Sister chromatids separate, producing two generally matching daughter cells. The human cycle uses mitosis for growth.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A division sequence that reduces two chromosome sets to one.
how: After one DNA replication, homologs separate in division I and sisters separate in division II.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The first meiotic division, which separates homologous chromosomes.
how: Pairing and crossing over precede homolog separation. The products are haploid with duplicated chromosomes.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The second meiotic division, which separates sister chromatids.
how: There is no second DNA replication beforehand. The general sequence ends with four haploid products.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The first stage of meiosis I, when homologs pair and crossing over occurs.
how: Corresponding homologs come together, allowing exchange between nonsister chromatids.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The stage when homologous pairs align at the cell equator.
how: Each pair’s orientation is independent, setting up alternative parental chromosome combinations.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The stage when homologous chromosomes move apart.
how: Each chromosome retains its joined sister chromatids while its homolog moves toward the other side.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The closing stage of the first meiotic division.
how: The simplified sequence forms two cells, each with one chromosome set and duplicated chromosomes.
memory: One set in each first-division product.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The beginning of the second meiotic division.
how: Division machinery forms without a new round of DNA replication.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The stage when individual chromosomes align in each haploid cell.
how: Their sister chromatids prepare to move to opposite sides of the cell.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The stage when sister chromatids separate.
how: The separated chromatids become the chromosomes of the daughter cells.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The closing stage of the second meiotic division.
how: Nuclei form, and the general sequence yields four haploid cells with unduplicated chromosomes.
memory: Four haploid products in the general model.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Exchange of corresponding DNA segments between nonsister chromatids.
how: During prophase I, chromatids from different homologs exchange DNA, creating new allele combinations.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Close pairing of homologous chromosomes during prophase I.
how: Pairing aligns corresponding regions before crossing over.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A visible crossover connection between homologous chromosomes.
how: It marks a connection associated with exchanged nonsister chromatids. It is distinct from the centromere.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Independent orientation of homologous chromosome pairs at metaphase I.
how: Alternative orientations mix whole maternal and paternal chromosomes across gametes. Two pairs allow four possible types across orientations.
memory: Each pair makes its own orientation choice.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A change in a DNA sequence.
how: Mutation can create new alleles. Sexual reproduction reshuffles alleles that already exist.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Differences that can pass from parents to offspring.
how: Natural selection can act on inherited differences associated with survival and reproduction.
memory: Heritable means it can be inherited.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A process in which some heritable variants become more common through differences in reproductive success.
how: It acts on variation rather than creating the new alleles itself. The seedlings are a conceptual illustration.
memory: Selection changes which inherited variants become common.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Differences in genetic information among individuals.
how: Mutation adds alleles, while assortment, crossing over and fertilization create combinations.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Reproduction involving the combination of genetic contributions through gametes.
how: The sperm-and-egg example illustrates new combinations in offspring.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Reproduction from one parent without fusion of gametes.
how: Hydra budding illustrates offspring that are usually clones of the parent.
memory: One parent supplies the starting information.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A genetically matching copy or group derived from the same source.
how: The slides say asexual offspring are usually clones. That qualifier avoids claiming perfect identity in every case.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A reproductive cell that can develop without fusing with another gamete.
how: In the plant pattern shown, meiosis produces haploid spores that lead to the gametophyte generation.
memory: A spore can grow without fertilization.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The diploid multicellular generation in the plant life cycle.
how: It produces haploid spores by meiosis in the pattern shown.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The haploid multicellular generation in the plant life cycle.
how: It produces gametes by mitosis, because it already has one chromosome set.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Coming from the mother.
how: The diagrams use one colour to track the chromosome contribution from the mother.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Coming from the father.
how: The second colour tracks the chromosome contribution from the father. Colours mark origin, not different chromosome types.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: An observable characteristic or trait.
how: The thought question links inherited differences in traits with natural selection.
memory: Phenotype is the trait you can observe or measure.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A small barrel-shaped cell structure, usually within a centrosome.
how: It is a cell structure, not the position of a gene on a chromosome.
memory: Centriole is not a gene address.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A region of the nucleus involved in making and assembling ribosomes.
how: It is a cell structure, so it is a distractor in the locus question.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A cell structure that makes proteins using RNA instructions.
how: It is different from a chromosome and from a gene’s locus.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: Having four complete chromosome sets.
how: A distractor uses 4n. Ordinary DNA replication in the lesson does not turn a 2n cell into a 4n cell.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The compartment containing chromosomes in a eukaryotic cell.
how: Nuclei form at the closing stage of the meiotic sequence shown.
memory: The nucleus contains the chromosome packages.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: The division machinery that helps move chromosomes.
how: The lesson notes spindle formation in prophase II and movement of chromatids later.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.

simple: A specialised chromosome region where division machinery attaches.
how: Sister chromatids are held together around this region. A chiasma instead connects homologs after crossing over.
memory: Centromere and chiasma mean different connections.
source: A short teaching explanation supplementing the supplied slides. NHGRI terminology reference where applicable.
